reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A self-limiting linear inflammatory dermatosis that follows the lines of Blaschko, typically as a continuous or interrupted band running down a limb
Most common in children and often appears abruptly over days to weeks
Comprises small pink, tan, or hypopigmented flat-topped papules that may become confluent and scaly
Usually unilateral and solitary, most often on a limb but occasionally on the trunk, neck, or face
Nail involvement can occur when the band crosses a digit, causing ridging, splitting, or onycholysis
Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation is common and may be the most conspicuous residual feature in darker skin, persisting after the papules settle
Thought to reflect a T-cell response against a clone of cutaneous cells carrying a post-zygotic (mosaic) mutation expressed along Blaschko's lines
Generally needs only reassurance and emollients, with topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors used for itch
reference.pathophysiology: Lichen striatus is believed to arise when an acquired trigger (possibly viral or environmental) provokes a T-lymphocyte-mediated reaction directed against a mosaic population of epidermal cells carrying a somatic mutation acquired during embryogenesis. Because these mutant clones are distributed along the developmental lines of Blaschko, the resulting lichenoid inflammation produces the characteristic linear band. The interface and sometimes spongiotic inflammation, often extending around adnexal structures deep in the dermis, damages the epidermis and disturbs pigmentation, accounting for the papules and the frequent residual hypopigmentation.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition of the Blaschko-linear distribution, which is usually sufficient for diagnosis
Skin biopsy in atypical cases showing lichenoid and sometimes spongiotic change with a deep peri-adnexal infiltrate
Wood's lamp examination to delineate the extent of post-inflammatory hypopigmentation
Nail examination and, if needed, nail-unit biopsy where there is dystrophy
Photographic follow-up to confirm spontaneous resolution
redFlags: Persistent or spreading linear lesions that do not resolve, prompting reconsideration of ILVEN or linear lichen planus
Atypical widespread or bilateral distribution requiring biopsy
reference.prognosis: Excellent; most cases resolve spontaneously within months to about a year, although post-inflammatory hypopigmentation and nail changes may take longer to normalise.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for linear lichen planus or ILVEN, which run more chronic courses
Attributing the residual hypopigmentation to vitiligo
Over-treating what is a self-limiting condition
management: Reassure that the condition is benign and self-resolving, so active treatment is often unnecessary
Use emollients for dryness and scaling
Apply topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors for itch or inflammation
Explain that post-inflammatory hypopigmentation fades slowly and needs no specific therapy
Monitor and manage nail dystrophy where the band crosses a digit
Arrange photographic follow-up to confirm spontaneous resolution and refer to dermatology for atypical or persistent cases
